title: The design of window shades and fenestration for view clarity
review_question: To better understand how shades can be designed so as to retain the window view, considering the influence of shading solutions, view content, and observer properties on view clarity.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: A narrative review of building standards and the scientific literature.

findings.antecedent: Fabric shading solutions (e.g., roller blinds) with high spatial frequency view content (e.g., nature)
findings.quote: Reduces high spatial frequency (e.g. nature) and retains low spatial frequency (e.g. urban) view content

findings.antecedent: Light-coloured fabric shades exposed to direct daylight
findings.quote: Light fabrics increase parasitic luminance when exposed to direct daylight and shade can become the new glare source.

findings.antecedent: Darker fabric shades
findings.quote: Darker fabrics reduce this effect and improve clarity, but the fabric will have a low surface albedo that could overheat the space

findings.antecedent: Shading patterns (e.g., horizontal blinds) that coincide with the composition of the view (e.g., horizontal layers)
findings.quote: Shading patterns (e.g. horizontal blinds) that coincide with the composition of the view (e.g. horizontal layers) significantly reduce view clarity and can evoke visual stress

findings.antecedent: Shades impeding areas where the three view layers (ground, landscape, sky) meet
findings.quote: Impeding areas where the three layers meet can fracture the view. Distant views have an elevated risk of being obscured as the landscape will appear smaller and there is a greater chance shades will block this layer

findings.antecedent: Immobile solid shading solutions (e.g., grills, automated rotatable louvres)
findings.quote: Reductions to view clarity are generally more permanent. This includes automated shades (e.g. rotatable louvres)

findings.antecedent: Glazing solutions with high tint state (e.g., electrochromic glass)
findings.consequent: Luminance contrast across window and view clarity
findings.quote: High luminance contrast across window will be reduced and view clarity is improved. However, interior reflections on glass can reduce clarity if room has strong interior lighting and light colours.

findings.antecedent: Tinted glazing and view content colour
findings.consequent: Ability to see certain colours in the view and view clarity
findings.quote: May improve or reduce the ability to see certain colours in the view. The level of view clarity will depend on the tint colour of the glass and dominant colour of the view content

findings.antecedent: Translucent obstructions (e.g., frosted glass)
findings.quote: Some types of glass may be selected to deliberately reduce view clarity (e.g. frost glass) for privacy, but still allow daylight into the room (e.g. bathrooms)

findings.antecedent: High view clarity (unobstructed fully glazed facades)
findings.quote: A significant drawback of high view clarity is the increased likelihood of bird collisions.

findings.antecedent: Shades that reduce glare or overheating beyond minimum acceptable levels of comfort
findings.consequent: Occupant preference for shades and view clarity
findings.quote: Shades that reduce glare or overheating beyond minimum acceptable levels of comfort are not preferred, since they offset other requirements such as view clarity.

findings.antecedent: High Openness Factor (OF) fabric shades
findings.quote: High values of Tv,n-n (typical of high OF) generally allow better shape recognition

findings.antecedent: Light-coloured fabric shades (high Tv,n-dif)
findings.quote: high values of Tv,n-dif (typical of light colours) distort the view and generate a parasitic luminance on the fabric

findings.antecedent: Darker fabric shades
findings.consequent: Reflected transmittance and visibility of direct daylight (view content)
findings.quote: Darker fabrics reduced the reflected transmittance between the fabric warp to allow the transmission of direct daylight, containing view content, to be more easily seen through the fabric.

findings.antecedent: Electrochromic glazing solutions
findings.quote: Electrochromic glazing solutions will generally ensure higher view clarity than roller blinds. Electrochromic glazing is able to preserve distant views, and fewer incidents of eyestrain and headaches have been attributed to the visual relief.

findings.antecedent: Window films and electrochromic glazing
findings.quote: However, window films and electrochromic glazing can reduce chromatic acuity (e.g. colour discrimination).

findings.antecedent: Blue-tinted spectacles
findings.quote: Shaik et al.67 found the greatest performance reductions were caused by blue-tinted spectacles

findings.antecedent: Yellow tints (lenses)
findings.consequent: Contrast for bright content against a blue background
findings.quote: yellow tints improve contrast for bright content against a blue background

findings.antecedent: Visual camouflage or masking (similarities in colour, brightness, pattern between shades and view content)
findings.consequent: Loss in outdoor content and view clarity
findings.quote: visual camouflage or masking results in a loss in outdoor content, particularly when the geometric characteristics of a window shade or fenestration (e.g. perforated meshes) coincide with the prevailing texture of the view.

findings.antecedent: Nature view content (high spatial frequency patterns)
findings.consequent: Visual information processing efficiency and comfort
findings.quote: Scenes with nature contain high-frequency patterns and less nuanced colours, allowing the eye to process visual information more efficiently and comfortably.

findings.antecedent: Urban environments (low spatial frequencies, abrupt contrast of unnatural colours)
findings.consequent: Visual information processing efficiency and comfort
findings.quote: Urban environments often have low spatial frequencies, which often exhibit unnaturally larger variations in colour.

findings.antecedent: Distant view content
findings.consequent: Visual angle and obstruction risk by shades
findings.quote: Distant content is mostly concentrated within the landscape layer (Figure 7), which gauges the distance of the view. Faraway landscape layers have a smaller visual angle and a higher chance of shades obstructing the content.

findings.antecedent: Increased distance of objects from observer
findings.consequent: Contrast and clarity (due to atmospheric perspective)
findings.quote: Atmospheric perspective will also decrease contrast at increased distances (i.e. the farther an object is from an observer the lower its clarity due to the molecules and particles in the air).

findings.antecedent: Blue-tinted films
findings.consequent: Ability to see blue visual stimuli and perception of sky/blue spaces
findings.quote: studies have shown that blue-tinted films hinder our ability to see blue visual stimuli. This could affect how the sky or blue spaces are perceived.

findings.antecedent: Yellow filters (compared to no filter)
findings.consequent: Contrast sensitivity (under photopic vision) and perceived brightness
findings.quote: Yap92 generally showed that contrast sensitivity was improved at most spatial frequencies under photopic vision when a yellow filter was compared to no filter. This could be due to the 40% increase in perceived brightness yellow filters create

findings.antecedent: Observer's visual acuity, psychological state (e.g., mood), and individual differences
findings.quote: Lastly, view clarity can depend on the visual acuity, psychological state of the observer and individual differences.

findings.antecedent: Age (≥60 years)
findings.consequent: Sensitivity to high spatial frequencies (e.g., nature content)
findings.quote: Older observers (≥60 years) have a lower sensitivity to frequencies above 4 cycles per degree. Therefore, elderly occupants may not be able to see high-frequency content (e.g. nature)

findings.antecedent: Colour blindness (e.g., red-green deficiency)
findings.consequent: Ability to see coloured view content and view quality
findings.quote: This means that people with colour blindness may have a reduced view quality.

findings.antecedent: Interior lighting exceeding exterior lighting (at night)
findings.quote: External views into the building are much clearer to render when interior lighting exceeds exterior lighting, posing an increased privacy issue.

synthesis_conclusions: View clarity is defined as the ability to see and discern view content through windows, influenced by obstruction properties, view content properties, and observer properties.
These three dimensions and their interactions significantly influence view clarity, making a single predictive model difficult.
Fabric shades reduce high spatial frequency content (e.g., nature) and can cause parasitic luminance, especially light-coloured fabrics in direct sunlight.
Solid shades, particularly those with patterns that visually camouflage with the view or are immobile, can permanently reduce view clarity and cause visual stress.
Glazing solutions (e.g., electrochromic glass) can improve view clarity and reduce eyestrain, but some (e.g., tinted films) may reduce chromatic acuity or distort specific colours.
View content properties like spatial frequency (nature vs. urban) and distance (nearby vs. distant) significantly impact how shades affect clarity.
Observer characteristics, including visual acuity, age-related decline in contrast sensitivity, and colour vision deficiencies, modulate perceived view clarity.
High view clarity has drawbacks, such as increased bird collisions, and can conflict with privacy needs, especially at night.
evidence_gaps: Current green certification labels for shading do not mention view clarity.
View clarity is largely understudied and not well understood.
The underlying relationships between obstruction, view content, and observer properties have not been applied to view clarity.
A comprehensive guidance for designers to follow regarding view clarity is lacking.
The View Clarity Index (VCI) does not consider every shade type or the dynamic operation of certain shades.
The conceptual dynamic view quality metric for dynamic shading has yet to be calibrated by human-subject experimentation to verify its accuracy.
Research on how colour blindness impacts view clarity is lacking.
It is not clear if glazing solutions will invariably retain high clarity for every view, as it depends on glass colour and view content.
limitations: The review is narrative, meaning it does not follow a systematic protocol for evidence selection and synthesis.
The complex interplay between obstruction properties, view content, and observer properties makes it difficult to predict view clarity for all situations.
The VCI metric does not cover all shade types or dynamic operations.
The review acknowledges that some design characteristics (e.g., reduced daylight illuminance) were not directly covered but are still important for a holistic outlook.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: The design of window shades and fenestration for view clarity
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
The ability to discern the content of the view through a window is referred to as
                    view clarity
                    . It is often overlooked in the design process, and the methods of shading daylight can affect window views. We conducted a narrative review of building standards and the scientific literature to better understand how shades can be designed so as to retain the window view. View clarity was characterised by three main dimensions: (1) the shading solution, (2) the view content and (3) the observer. Each dimension and the interactions between them influence view clarity. These interactions make it difficult to predict view clarity for all the situations that can occur in buildings. Nonetheless, we highlighted the effects of different shades on the view clarity. Our insights can help designers consider these impacts within the context of overall window design.
